questions.question: What does chmod 600 notes.txt allow?
options: Everyone can read and write
The owner can execute only
Only the owner can read and write
The group can read and execute
questions.explanation: 6 grants read (4) plus write (2) to the owner. Both zeroes remove permissions for the group and others.

questions.question: Which signal does kill send by default?
options: SIGKILL
SIGTERM
SIGSTOP
SIGHUP
questions.explanation: kill sends SIGTERM by default. A process can handle this signal to shut down gracefully, unlike SIGKILL.

questions.question: What does the pipe operator | normally connect?
options: A command’s standard output to the next command’s standard input
Two files into a directory
A command’s exit code to the next command’s arguments
All output streams to a log file
questions.explanation: A normal pipe connects standard output to standard input. Standard error remains separate unless explicitly redirected.

questions.question: In Bash, what does this print?
options: A syntax error
The literal text $name
Ada
An empty line
questions.explanation: Single quotes prevent parameter expansion. Double quotes would allow the variable to expand while preserving the resulting text as one argument.

questions.question: Why quote "$path" when passing a possibly space-containing pathname to a command?
options: To prevent word splitting and pathname expansion of its value
To force the file to be executable
To encrypt the path
To resolve symbolic links automatically
questions.explanation: Quoting keeps an expanded pathname as one argument. Unquoted expansion can split it into words or interpret wildcard characters.

questions.question: Inside a Bash function, which expansion preserves each original positional argument as a separate word?
options: Unquoted $*
questions.explanation: Quoted "$@" expands each positional argument separately. Quoted "$*" joins them into one word using the first IFS character.

questions.question: In Bash, what is the exit status of this pipeline?
options: Always 127
Zero because true is the last command
The text false
Nonzero because pipefail exposes the failure
questions.explanation: With pipefail, a pipeline returns the status of its rightmost failing command, or zero if none fail.

questions.question: Assume stdout initially goes to a terminal. Where does stderr go here?
options: It is discarded
To the original stdout destination, normally the terminal
Into out.log together with stdout
Into a file named 1
questions.explanation: Redirections are processed left to right. stderr is duplicated from the original stdout before stdout is redirected.

questions.question: Which redirection appends stdout without truncating an existing log?
options: command 2<app.log
command >>app.log
command >app.log
command <app.log
questions.explanation: The >> operator opens the destination for appending. A single > normally truncates an existing regular file.

questions.question: What does this command discard?
options: Standard error only
Standard output only
The input file contents
Both stdout and stderr
questions.explanation: File descriptor 2 is stderr. Redirecting it to /dev/null leaves stdout unchanged.

questions.question: What does execute permission on a directory primarily allow?
options: Listing all its entries without read permission
Executing every file inside it regardless of file permissions
Changing its owner
Searching or traversing that directory
questions.explanation: Directory execute permission permits pathname traversal. Listing entries requires directory read permission; file access also depends on other applicable checks.

questions.question: Ignoring sticky bits, ACLs, and other restrictions, what permissions usually allow deleting a file from a directory?
options: Write permission on the file alone
Write and execute permissions on the containing directory
Execute permission on the file alone
Ownership of the file is always mandatory
questions.explanation: Unlinking changes the directory entry. Permission to modify a file’s contents is distinct from permission to remove its name from a directory.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the sticky bit on a shared directory such as /tmp?
options: Encrypt all new files
Prevent files from being read by their owners
Make every file executable
Restrict who can remove or rename entries despite shared write access
questions.explanation: In a sticky directory, removal and renaming are restricted to appropriately privileged users, the file owner, or the directory owner.

questions.question: Assuming a program requests mode 0666 for a new regular file and no default ACL changes the result, what does umask 027 produce?
questions.explanation: The umask removes permission bits from the requested mode. It does not add execute bits to a regular file requested with 0666.

questions.question: What is a common effect of setting the setgid bit on a Linux directory?
options: Every new file becomes owned by root
All files become immutable
New entries inherit the directory’s group ownership
Group members automatically gain sudo access
questions.explanation: Setgid directories support shared group ownership for new entries. Access permissions remain governed by modes, ACLs, and the creating process.

questions.question: You create a hard link to a regular file, then unlink the original name. What happens to the data?
options: The remaining name contains only a backup snapshot
It is immediately deleted from both names
The hard link becomes a symbolic link
It remains accessible through the other hard link
questions.explanation: Hard links refer to the same inode. Storage is reclaimed only when no links and no relevant open references remain.

questions.question: How does a symbolic link differ from a hard link?
options: It stores a target pathname and can point across filesystems
It guarantees the target will always exist
It always shares the target inode
It cannot point to a directory
questions.explanation: A symbolic link resolves a pathname and may dangle if its target disappears. Hard links bind another name to the same filesystem object.

questions.question: df shows a nearly full filesystem, but du finds much less usage. Which situation can explain this?
options: All files have read-only permissions
The filesystem has no directories
The shell has an empty PATH
A process still holds a large deleted file open
questions.explanation: Unlinked but open files still occupy storage until their open references are released. Tools such as lsof can help identify them.

questions.question: New file creation fails with No space left on device, but many bytes remain free. What should you check?
options: The current Git branch
Only the CPU load average
Free inodes using df -i
Whether /etc/hosts contains localhost
questions.explanation: Filesystems can exhaust inodes before exhausting data blocks. Byte-capacity and inode-capacity checks diagnose different limits.

questions.question: Why pair these options when processing arbitrary filenames?
options: They sort files by inode number
They remove execute permissions first
They preserve filenames containing whitespace or newlines
They prevent every race condition
questions.explanation: NUL separators preserve pathname boundaries. This handles unusual filenames but is not a universal defense against filesystem races.

questions.question: With GNU grep, what does exit status 1 normally mean?
options: A match was found
The file was encrypted
No matching lines were selected
The pattern was automatically corrected
questions.explanation: GNU grep normally returns zero for a selected match, one for no match, and two for an error. Scripts should distinguish absence from execution failure.

questions.question: Why does this command sort before using uniq -c?
options: The pipe converts line counts to bytes
uniq requires alphabetical input or it crashes
uniq groups adjacent identical lines, so sorting brings duplicates together
sort removes all duplicate lines by itself
questions.explanation: uniq only combines adjacent equal lines. Sorting is a common way to group identical lines before counting them.

questions.question: What does this awk command print for a normal colon-separated /etc/passwd entry?
options: The last character of each line
The first field, typically the account name
The numeric user ID only
The complete line with colons removed
questions.explanation: -F selects the field separator and $1 references the first field.

questions.question: Does this sed command modify config.txt in place?
options: No; it writes transformed text to stdout
Yes, it overwrites the input automatically
It deletes config.txt after reading it
Yes, but only the first line
questions.explanation: Without an in-place editing option or explicit output handling, sed writes its transformed stream to stdout.

questions.question: What does tar -czf backup.tar.gz app/ normally do?
options: Creates a gzip-compressed archive containing app/
Lists open network sockets
Extracts an archive into app/
Changes the owner of app/ recursively
questions.explanation: c creates an archive, z uses gzip, and f selects the archive filename. Extraction would use x instead of c.

questions.question: What does systemctl enable app.service do without --now?
options: Rewrites the service executable
Configures activation links according to the unit’s installation settings
Restarts the service every minute
Starts the service immediately in all cases
questions.explanation: Enabling and starting a unit are separate operations. Use --now when you intend to enable and start together.

questions.question: After editing a systemd unit file, which operation makes the manager reread unit definitions?
options: systemctl reload app.service always rereads all unit files
systemctl reset-failed only
systemctl daemon-reload
journalctl --rotate
questions.explanation: daemon-reload reloads unit configuration and dependencies. A service reload requests application-specific reload behavior instead.

questions.question: What logs does this command request?
options: The contents of the unit’s environment variables
Only messages from the previous boot
Every file under /var/log
Journal entries for app.service from the current boot
questions.explanation: -u filters by unit and -b restricts output to the selected boot, the current boot by default.

questions.question: What does /proc/<PID>/fd contain on Linux?
options: Only TCP connection passwords
The process’s executable source code
Entries representing that process’s open file descriptors
Copies of every file ever opened
questions.explanation: These entries link to open file descriptions such as files, pipes, and sockets. Access depends on permissions and process visibility restrictions.

questions.question: What is a zombie process?
options: An exited process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status
A process that cannot be listed by ps
A process using all available CPU
A process waiting for keyboard input
questions.explanation: A zombie retains minimal process-table information until reaped. Sending it SIGKILL does not make it exit again.

questions.question: In ps output, what does state D commonly indicate on Linux?
options: A daemon that is guaranteed healthy
Uninterruptible sleep, often related to I/O
A process with deleted source code
A successfully completed process
questions.explanation: D commonly indicates an uninterruptible kernel wait. Investigate the underlying I/O or kernel wait rather than assuming CPU contention.

questions.question: For ordinary Linux scheduling, what does a higher numeric nice value generally mean?
options: Higher real-time priority
Lower CPU scheduling priority relative to less-nice competitors
Guaranteed exclusive CPU access
A larger memory limit
questions.explanation: Niceness influences fair-scheduler priority. It is not a memory limit or a guarantee of a particular CPU percentage.

questions.question: What does kill -0 <PID> do?
options: Terminates the process with status zero
Resets its CPU usage counters
Pauses the process for zero seconds
Checks process existence and signaling permission without delivering a signal
questions.explanation: Signal zero performs permission and existence checks. Failure may reflect insufficient permission rather than absence alone.

questions.question: What does nohup primarily change?
options: It guarantees the process survives all failures
It arranges for the command to ignore SIGHUP
It turns the command into a systemd unit
It automatically backgrounds every command
questions.explanation: nohup addresses hangup-signal handling and may redirect terminal output. Use & separately to run a shell job in the background.

questions.question: In a clean Bash session where LAB_VALUE was not previously exported, why does this child shell print an empty line?
options: A child shell always inherits every parent variable
Bash variable names cannot contain lowercase letters
Single quotes delete the parent variable
The variable was not exported into the child environment
questions.explanation: Shell variables are not automatically environment variables. export makes a variable available in subsequently launched child processes.

questions.question: How can a shell script set a variable in the current Bash session?
options: Source the script in that session
Run it through nohup
Pipe it into any external command
Execute it as a separate process normally
questions.explanation: source or . executes commands in the current shell context. A normal child process cannot directly modify its parent shell’s environment.

questions.question: What does Bash command substitution remove from captured standard output?
options: Trailing newline characters
The first line only
Every newline including internal ones
All spaces
questions.explanation: $(...) replaces itself with command output after removing trailing newlines. Quoting the expansion still matters for argument boundaries.

questions.question: If port is unset, what value is printed?
options: A syntax error
The literal text port:-8080
An empty string
questions.explanation: The :- parameter expansion supplies a default when the parameter is unset or null. It does not assign that default to the variable.

questions.question: When is cleanup executed in this list?
options: Always, regardless of build’s status
Before build starts
Only if build exits with status zero
Only if build fails
questions.explanation: && executes its right-hand command only after a successful left-hand command. It is not equivalent to a finally block.

questions.question: What is a common purpose of set -u in Bash scripts?
options: Treat many expansions of unset variables as errors
Disable variable expansion entirely
Force all variables to be integers
Stop on every possible command failure
questions.explanation: nounset helps catch missing variables. It is distinct from errexit and has exceptions for certain special parameters and expansion forms.

questions.question: A command works interactively but not in cron because a helper executable cannot be found. What is a likely cause?
options: Cron deletes executables before starting jobs
Cron has a different or minimal PATH
The command must be stored in /tmp
Cron always runs in the user’s interactive login shell
questions.explanation: Scheduled jobs often have a limited environment. Set required paths explicitly or use suitable absolute executable paths.

questions.question: What does this command show?
options: Listening TCP sockets with numeric addresses and ports
All files owned by root
A route table with DNS names
Only established UDP sessions
questions.explanation: ss reports socket information; -l selects listening sockets, -t selects TCP, and -n disables name resolution.

questions.question: Which command helps determine the route and source address Linux would use for a specific destination?
options: systemctl route 203.0.113.10
ip route get 203.0.113.10
questions.explanation: ip route get asks the kernel to resolve a route lookup. It helps distinguish routing decisions from DNS resolution problems.

questions.question: Why can getent hosts app.example differ from a direct DNS query tool?
options: getent always ignores /etc/hosts
getent only reads the Git configuration
getent follows the system’s configured name-service sources
DNS tools modify /etc/nsswitch.conf
questions.explanation: The system resolver may consult sources such as files and DNS according to name-service configuration. A direct DNS query does not reproduce every NSS lookup path.

questions.question: A server returns HTTP 404. With curl --fail, what normally happens?
options: curl retries forever until the page exists
curl reports a nonzero exit status for that HTTP error
curl changes the response to 200
curl reports success because the TCP connection worked
questions.explanation: --fail makes HTTP error responses produce a failure status. Transport success and application-level HTTP success are different concepts.

questions.question: What does curl -k disable for HTTPS requests?
options: All TLS encryption
The HTTP Host header
TCP connection establishment
Certificate verification checks
questions.explanation: -k skips certificate verification, weakening server identity checks. It does not disable encryption and is not the correct fix for a trust-chain problem.

questions.question: An SSH private key is readable by other users and OpenSSH refuses it. What is an appropriate first fix?
options: Disable host-key checking
Make the key world-writable
Restrict its permissions so only its owner can read it
Copy the private key into authorized_keys on every host
questions.explanation: OpenSSH protects private keys from unsafe file permissions. Owner-only access such as mode 600 is appropriate for a typical private key file.

questions.question: A process reports Too many open files. Which limit and usage should you inspect?
options: Only its disk byte quota
Only its nice value
The number of lines in /etc/passwd
Its open descriptor count and RLIMIT_NOFILE
questions.explanation: Open files include sockets and pipes as well as regular files. A descriptor leak can exhaust the per-process open-file limit.

questions.question: Writes fail with Read-only file system even though file permissions allow writing. What should you inspect?
options: Only the file’s extension
The mount’s read-only state and filesystem error logs
Whether the current shell is interactive
The DNS search domain
questions.explanation: Filesystem mount state can prevent writes independently of permission bits. Some filesystems remount read-only after serious errors.

questions.question: In Bash, why is -eq appropriate in this test?
options: It compares integer values rather than lexicographic string order
It expands a regular expression
It tests whether a file exists
It assigns n to 10
questions.explanation: The test command’s -eq operator compares integers. String equality uses a different operator and does not perform numeric comparison.
